claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The reported HfNbTiVAl10 microstructure is dendritic.
The hierarchical, dendritic state was produced by arc melting under inert conditions.
Dendrite size, chemical-fluctuation amplitude, and phase distribution can serve as quantitative descriptors of the hierarchical microstructure.
Hierarchical-microstructure metrics directly influence dislocation mobility.
Hierarchical-microstructure metrics directly influence crack initiation.
The hierarchical microstructure mediates the relationship between composition and processing and the resulting mechanical performance.
Valence-electron-concentration effects influence dislocation mobility and slip activity.
Combining microstructure descriptors with composition-based physical rules constrains the machine-learning model to physically relevant limits.
Physics-based constraints enable faster model convergence.
The hybrid framework reduces reliance on computationally intensive atomistic simulations.
A microstructure-informed framework can capture the effects of chemical heterogeneity and dendritic structure on dislocation behavior and work hardening.
Capturing microstructural effects on dislocation behavior and work hardening improves prediction of toughness.
The hybrid framework will reduce computational time by at least 50% relative to pure CALPHAD, DFT, or rule-of-mixtures approaches.
The hybrid framework will reduce prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional methods.
Full first-principles and CALPHAD approaches are computationally demanding.
Composition-based models and full first-principles or CALPHAD approaches have limited toughness-prediction capability because they insufficiently incorporate microstructural effects.
The method is expected to remain reliable for as-cast HfNbTiVAl10 that retains its hierarchical heterostructure.
Significant post-casting modification of the hierarchical features may make the method unreliable.
Large deviations in temperature or strain rate from the training-data conditions may make the method unreliable.
